doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Jazz parties: Otter Crest and the aging audience
summary: He recalls his first jazz party at Otter Crest in Oregon, the older white audience, the repertoire demanded and the quality of the players.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Excellent. These jazz parties — when was the first time you did a jazz party?
I think the first one I ever did was Otter Crest, which I don’t know, have you ever heard of Otter Crest?

Oh it’s a wonderful one. It was up in Salem, Oregon, run by Bill and Mary Brown, and it was in this gorgeous setting overlooking the Pacific. What a beautiful party. And all of a sudden all these wonderful players come from all over and we’d get together in this idyllic little resort, overlooking the Pacific, and there are seals down on the rocks down below and stuff, and just that northern coastline — the northern California/Oregon coastline, which is overwhelming to a person from the east who’s never really seen that, how different and how expansive and beautiful it is. And all these musicians from the west coast would come up and the guys on the east coast would get together and they’d have some really good sets. I mean it wasn’t just traditional music, it was a lot of real swing — it never got past really swing, I mean a little bop maybe, it never got modern, modern. But they’re catering to the audience, which at that time was mostly white people from 50 on. So you know you play the music they want if you want customers. It’s the old customer thing you know.
As it is at most of them.
In fact you see a lot of the same faces. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

And they’re getting older, and they’re dying off, and I don’t know what it’s going to be with this kind of thing, but it’s all right. There’s no younger faces here. There’s no younger people getting interested in this music. But they are certainly interested in their music. There is lots of music there, so we’ll see what happens. I suspect there will always be a market for those of us who wish to play. The music that we’re playing at this festival isn’t exactly my cup of tea either. I mean while I love how — to miss New Orleans to [scats] — “Do you know what it means to miss New Orleans” — I can’t play it every night now, you know? I mean this homage to older jazz gets a little tiresome to me. But then it’s all right, because the players are great.
Every once in a while it’s fun to play that I guess.
And watch the group on stage work things out. I mean there’s a lot of horn players up there.

Yeah, and these guys, these guys know how to — I mean I’m not just saying it to cover my bases, cover my tracks here, but these guys are very good, I mean Peplowski and well, I guess maybe there’s no sense listing them, but they’re all very good players, and it’s been a lot of fun. They know what they’re doing. These are the pros of the pros in this business downstairs right now. They know just how to do it.
